findings.issue: Step 8 instructs to configure CORS with `allowedOrigins("${app.url:http://localhost:3000}")` (line 63). This is a Spring property placeholder syntax — it is NOT resolved when passed as a Java string literal to the allowedOrigins() method. The CORS origin will literally be the string '${app.url:http://localhost:3000}', which will never match any real browser origin, silently breaking CORS for all requests. SecurityConfig must @Value-inject the app.url property and pass the injected field value to allowedOrigins().
findings.fix: Change the CORS instruction to: 'Inject app URL via constructor/field: @Value("${app.url:http://localhost:3000}") String appUrl. Then call allowedOrigins(appUrl) in the CORS config.' The placeholder must be in the @Value annotation on a field, not as a string literal argument.

findings.issue: Implementation hint (line 138) says: 'MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") is not thread-safe; create a new instance per call or use DigestUtils from Spring.' Spring's org.springframework.util.DigestUtils only provides MD5 digest utilities — it has no SHA-256 method. Suggesting it as an alternative to MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") is a hallucinated API reference. An implementer who tries to use Spring's DigestUtils for SHA-256 will find no such method and may import Apache Commons Codec's DigestUtils (different library, not in dependencies) by mistake.
findings.fix: Remove 'or use DigestUtils from Spring' from the hint. Correct hint: 'MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") is not thread-safe; create a new instance per call. Spring Security's org.springframework.security.crypto.codec.Hex can encode the resulting byte[] to a hex string.'
